challenges.name: lists-low-end-phones-quiz
challenges.title: Read the janky delivery list
challenges.description: Three statements about what Rice Rocket measured when the delivery list stuttered on the Galaxy A03 phones most couriers use. Decide whether each one is true.
hints: React Native has a JS thread that runs your components and a UI thread that draws native views. Which of the two numbers dropped?
`windowSize` counts viewport heights kept rendered around the screen. What does the list show for a fast fling if almost nothing outside the screen is rendered?
A key tells React which component instance belongs to which item. After an insert at the top, what does index 5 point to?

questions.question:
The Perf Monitor while a courier scrolls "Today's deliveries" on a Galaxy A03:

```text
UI:  59.8 fps
JS:  11.2 fps   (frames dropped while scrolling)
RAM: 212 MB
```

Statement: "The native UI thread keeps up; the JS thread is the bottleneck, so the fix is less JavaScript work per row (fewer re-renders, cheaper rows), not faster native drawing."
questions.explanation: True. React Native renders your components on the JS thread and the UI thread draws the native views. A healthy UI rate next to a collapsed JS rate means the JavaScript side (rendering rows, re-rendering them, work in handlers) cannot produce updates fast enough; FlatList then shows blank areas until rows arrive. The misconception is that list jank is always a native drawing problem.

questions.question:
To cut the JS work, a teammate shrinks the render window:

```tsx
<FlatList data={items} renderItem={renderItem} windowSize={1} />
```

Statement: "`windowSize={1}` renders only the visible screen, so the list gets smoother with no visible side effect."
questions.explanation: False. `windowSize` is measured in viewport heights (the default is 21: the visible area plus 10 above and 10 below). With 1, nothing outside the screen is ready, so a fast fling shows blank space while rows are rendered on demand, and rows are mounted and unmounted constantly. A small window trades memory and work for blank areas; values like 5 to 11 with `getItemLayout` and memoized rows usually work better.

questions.question:
The list uses the position as key. Dispatch inserts a new delivery at the top while the courier has row 5 expanded:

```tsx
<FlatList data={items} keyExtractor={(_, index) => String(index)} ... />
```

```text
before: index 5 = d-5 (expanded)    after insert: index 5 = d-4, index 6 = d-5
screen: d-4 is now shown expanded; d-5 is collapsed
```

Statement: "Keying by `item.id` makes each component instance follow its delivery, so the expanded state stays on d-5 and only the new row has to render."
questions.explanation: True. React matches instances to items by key. With index keys, the instance that was showing d-5 now receives d-4's props: its local state (expanded) moves to the wrong delivery and every row after the insert re-renders with new props. With a stable id, existing instances keep their item and state; only the new delivery mounts. The misconception is that keys only matter for warnings.

challenges.name: delivery-list-config
challenges.title: Configure the delivery list for low-end phones
challenges.description: "Today's deliveries" is a FlatList of time-slot headers (40 px) and delivery rows (96 px). On low-end phones it measured every row while scrolling, re-rendered every visible row when one status changed, and after dispatch inserted a delivery, the courier's expanded row jumped to another delivery. The editor holds `listConfig(items, openDelivery)`, which builds the props the screen passes to FlatList and `React.memo`, with its key blocks missing, each marked by a `// [ ]` line; some pieces are wrong on purpose. Fill every line so that: `getItemLayout` returns each item's exact height and offset (headers and rows differ); keys follow the delivery, not its position; a row re-renders only when its own delivery changed; and the row's props stay equal between renders (`openDelivery` is already stable). Run models FlatList's render window and React's key matching, then counts rendered rows per update.
hints: For each update ask two things: which component instance does React match to each item (the key decides), and does `sameRow` see equal props for rows that did not change?
Look at the heights array and the running offset, `keyExtractor`'s two arguments, whether `rowProps` creates a new function each time, and what `sameRow` compares.

A chat screen with date separators (24 px) and messages (64 px) does: `heights = items.map((i) => (i.kind === "date" ? 24 : 64))`, a running sum for offsets, `keyExtractor={(m) => m.id}`, `React.memo(MessageRow, (a, b) => a.message === b.message && a.onLongPress === b.onLongPress)` with `onLongPress` from `useCallback`.

tests.name: getItemLayout gives exact offsets for headers and rows, and the right window mounts
A status change on one visible delivery re-renders that row only
A delivery inserted at the top: the expanded row stays on its delivery, one new row renders
Three status changes in a row near the end of the list
Insert below the expanded row, then a status change: no state moves, minimal renders
